newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-INDIAN BUDGET-GOOD ARITHMETIC BUT...-BY NATWEST.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-INDIAN BUDGET-GOOD ARITHMETIC BUT...-BY NATWEST.

text.p: The following is an excerpt from a budget preview by
securities firm NatWest Markets titled "Good Arithmetic But..."
Natwest forecasts a pro-growth, pro-infrastructure budget but says market expectations in the run up to February 28 are unlikely to be met.
Our estimate for the gross fiscal deficit (GFD) is a surprisingly benign 5.4 percent for FY97 and 4.7 percent for FY98.
Steep revisions of the FY95 and FY96 GDP numbers, postponement of pay hikes and reduction in plan capital expenditure have resulted in a tame deficit.
FY98 also looks like a comfortable year, we estimate the GFD to be around 4.7 percent of GDP. Thus, given that:
* the fiscal situation seems to be under control, the GFD will be contained at below 5 percent in FY98.
* the risk of an intransigent Congress is further out than earlier expected.
The UF government has now got the scope to deliver a growth oriented budget geared towards boosting business confidence.
The budget would focus on infrastructure (and the related debt market development) and simultaneously increase capital expenditure.
Fiscal consolidation will continue, with hikes in administered prices and reduction in subsidies.
BUDGET FY98 - FOCUS ON THE BASIC ISSUES
PHILOSOPHY: DEBT MARKET DEVELOPMENT AND INFRASTRUCTURE
POLICY INITIATIVE:
** Development of an active inter-bank borrowing rate, by abolishing CRR and SLR on such borrowings.
** Incentives to encourage long term contractual savings (for example, pension and provident funds and insurance).
** Deregulate insurance and pension funds, increase competition and ease the investment norms of these funds to improve returns.
** The benefits under section 36(1)(viii), currently availed by the FIs, are likely to be extended to the banks involved in long-term infrastructure and agricultural finance.
** Tax holiday for green field infrastructure projects.
** Enhance investment ceiling on infrastructure debt under section 88, and to increase the limit of section 80L benefit on interest income from infrastructure debt.
** Double taxation of dividends may be removed for investments in infrastructure projects.
IMPLICATIONS:
As the investment norms of the PFs/ICs are likely to be eased over the year, capital receipts from these institutions in the Union Budget would be moderated in FY98.
PHILOSOPHY: INVESTMENT CONFIDENCE
POLICY INITIATIVE:
** The 7.5 percent surcharge of corporate tax may be withdrawn.
** Steep reduction of customs duties may be ruled out in the FY98 budget, giving a breather to the domestic producers against international competition.
IMPLICATIONS:

Removal of the surcharge and double taxation will reduce receipts by around 18 billion rupees and 3 billion rupees respectively. However, the measure will go a long way towards boosting the confidence level.
PHILOSOPHY: FISCAL CONSOLIDATION
POLICY INITIATIVE:

** Revenue expenditure is likely to go up by 235 billion rupees approximately. Major subsidies are likely to go up by another 16 billion rupees (food subsidy) in FY98, inspite of the hike in administered prices of sugar, fertiliser, coal and oil.
** Fifth pay commission recommendations are unlikely to be accepted in full. We expect the increase in revenue expenditure to be around 88 billion rupees in FY98 (including past arrears).
** The government is likely to repay the oil pool account the amount that it had previously borrowed.
IMPLICATIONS:

** Domestic market borrowing of the government is not expected to increase by more than 10 billion rupees in FY98. Increase in the price of levy sugar will reduce subsidy on sugar by around 6 billion rupees. A 10 percent increase in urea prices will also reduce the subsidy on fertilisers by 5.5 billion rupees. Increase in administered prices will reduce overall implicit and explicit subsidies. The budgetary support to PSEs is not expected to increase in FY98. Removal of corporate surcharge will cost the government about 18 billion rupees.
** Capital expenditure will increase by 41 billion rupees if the goverment decides to repay the 'Oil pool', the amount it borrowed in 1991.
PHILOSOPHY: SOCIAL SPENDING
POLICY INITIATIVE:
** Increased allocation for employment, education, housing, sanitation, rural development etc.
IMPLICATIONS:
The budget would largely do lip service in terms of social spending. We do not expect the budgetary allocation to be increased by more than 15 billion rupees.
PHILOSOPHY: BROADENING OF THE TAX BASE
POLICY INITIATIVE:
** There may be a decrease in the marginal rate of taxation at the lower slabs to increase the base of income tax.

** The budget may widen the net of presumptive taxes on consumption expenditures by introducing/increasing taxes on miscellaneous services and expenditures (eg. registered automobiles, credit cards, club memberships, entertainment etc.)
IMPLICATIONS:

Widening of the direct tax base by lowering the tax rates is possible. However, it is likely that the targets set by the government will be over-optimistic. Presumptive taxes have not been very successful in the past, and there is no reason to be optimistic now.
PHILOSOPHY: EXPORT PROMOTION
POLICY INITIATIVE:

** The 2 percent additional import duty may be removed from imports of export related items, deemed exports and infrastructure related items and for capital imports under the (Export Promotion Council Group) EPCG scheme.
** Import duty of capital goods under the EPCG scheme may be reduced from 15 percent to 10 percent.
** Export earnings may be kept out of the net of MAT in FY98.
IMPLICATIONS:
Exports have suffered in FY97. These policy incentives will help revive exports.

RECEIPTS:
The revenue receipts will fall short of target in FY97 by about 40 billion rupees. Decelaration in industrial growth in 4QFY97 would lead to lower corporate tax and excise collections.
The government may still be optimistic about collections and put the gross fiscal deficit lower at 5.2 percent of GDP.
In FY98 we expect receipts to be buoyant as the economy is expected to register near 7 percent growth.
However, to what extent will the widening of the tax net be effective is questionable.

We have remained rather conservative in terms of our forecasts on income tax collections. We have also considered higher non tax revenue receipts in FY98 as the telecom license fees which did not come through in FY97 will reach the exchequer in Fy98 (13.5 billion rupees).
We have assumed higher external borrowings in FY98. The PSU disinvestment programme turned out to be a failure again in FY97, but we expect the government to keep a tall target again in FY98.
The government wants to test the international debt market, this would prepare a benchmark for the cost of funds for Indian corporates wishing to borrow abroad.
In case the government fails to borrow externally, the amount we have projected, the pressure will come to domestic market to that extent (assuming no monetisation).
EXPENDITURE:

The government will overshoot its revenue expenditure target in FY97 by 23 billion rupees. This is despite the fact that the government has not spent 40 billion rupees budgeted for the pay hike in FY97.
However, capital expenditure has been curtailed drastically, as a result overall expenditure in FY97 will be under control. Fiscal deficit will overshoot estimate because of shortfall in receipts.
In FY98 revenue expenditure will increase substantially, pay hikes including arrears will cost the centre around 88 billion rupees in FY98.
Increase in food subsidy will be in the region of 25 billion rupees. Besides we have also assumed that the centre will return, the previously borrowed, 41 billion rupees to the oil pool account.
Fiscal deficit may not decrease significantly in nominal terms, however, expressed as a percentage of GDP it will be below 5 percent.
GROWTH, INFLATION AND INTEREST RATES:
The manufacturing sector is going through a slowdown in 4QFY97. We expect consumption demand to improve in 1H97.

The budget will be overall positive to growth. Increase in capital expenditure, reasonable amount of government borrowings and some fiscal incentives will all act towards reviving business confidence.
Growth in manufacturing will revive in 2HFY98. With normal monsoons overall GDP growth in FY98 should be around 6.6 percent of GDP.
Inflation will remain well above 9 percent 1QFY98. We expect a 10 percent increase in the index of fuel prices after the revision in administered prices in FY98 budget.
The Railway freight rates are also likely to go up by 10 percent. While inflation pressure may ease in the second quarter, prices of manufactured products will again fuel inflation in 2HFY98.

Average inflation in FY98 will be around 8.5 percent. Interest rates are likely to remain subdued in 1HFY98. However, as the government borrowing will be aggressive in 1HFY98 and as credit demand improves there would be pressure on interest rates to go up.
If 5 percent of the incremental accruals to the PF corpus is freed as a result of easing of the investment norms, it would release 18 billion rupees for other investments in FY98.

To that extent, it would result in a pressure on the banks to subscribe in government paper. We expect banks to raise their prime lending rates (PLR) in August/September 1997. The PLR of banks may rise to 15.5 percent by the fiscal end.
